abstract: When exposed to stressful environmental conditions, adults of long-lived species may favour self-maintenance at the expense of reproductive investment. In breeding king penguins (Aptenodytes patagonicus), we previously showed that prolonged glucocorticoid hormone exposure during early breeding resulted in surprisingly little effect on parental self-maintenance. Here, we investigate whether the potential costs of this experimental stressor could be transferred to offspring through altered parental care, negatively affecting their growth, physiology and survival. We exposed parents to a ca. 1-month elevation in corticosterone and monitored parental investment and offspring performance over one year, from incubation to fledging. Corticosterone-treated parents exhibited reduced prolactin levels and spent less time at sea, highlighting alterations in both endocrine and behavioural processes supporting parental investment. Yet, parental care behaviour, hatching success and chick body mass/size were not significantly impacted. Major delayed costs of the parental treatment were however evident, as chicks from corticosterone-treated parents exhibited accelerated postnatal telomere shortening and faced nearly twice the mortality hazard of chicks from placebo-treated parents. By revealing the hidden reproductive costs of apparent parental resilience, our study challenges how we assess the consequences of environmental stressors in long-lived species, particularly when their effects only emerge long after exposure.
